item.title: Nvidia Asked to Sell Chips to Companies Tied to Chinese Military and Megaspeed
item.description:
Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced A.I. chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon.

The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as of that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 artificial intelligence chips for Alibaba, a Chinese A.I. giant that The New York Times reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory.

The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who U.S. intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia chief executive.

The company — New Century Lettall Data Service — is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Ms. Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Ms. Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director.

The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for the Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese A.I. firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said. They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chip maker AMD, the MI325X.

The lawmakers, from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems. The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the license requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centers.

Two Times reports first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Nvidia scandal.

Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed.

The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Ms. Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week. The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China.

The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China. Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticized the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating.

The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said.

John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said that the review and licensing process for the H200 spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. “Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” he said.

A spokeswoman for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance.

The Commerce Department did not reply to a request for comment.

President Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 percent tariff on their value and perform a security check.

Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms.

Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move.

In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest.” The committee plans to hold hearings next month with both Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications.

Representative Brian Mast, a Florida Republican and chairman of the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies,” and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us,” he said.

Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Democrat of New York, said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight.”

“Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said.

item.title: Delaware Regulator Says It Was ‘Misled’ About Mark Walter’s Insurance Assets
item.description:
Delaware’s insurance regulator said Thursday that it and many other regulators were “misled” about the classification of billions of dollars in assets held by two life insurance companies controlled by Mark Walter, the billionaire investor and owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The Delaware Department of Insurance also said in a lengthy statement that it was conducting its own investigation into the misclassification of assets; that inquiry comes on the heels of an investigation by federal prosecutors and federal securities regulators. In its statement the state agency rejected criticism of its oversight of the two firms, Delaware Life and Clear Spring, that has been raised by some industry analysts.

Both of the insurers, regulated in Delaware, disclosed earlier this year they were being investigated by federal authorities and had discovered that roughly $21 billion in assets they held should have been listed as investments with entities affiliated with other businesses tied to Mr. Walter and his TWG Global financial and sports empire.

The Delaware insurance department said it was misled about the true nature of these investments, and that the insurers, the auditor for the companies, and rating agencies were also misled. The statement did not comment on who had misled the regulator.

A spokesman for the insurers declined to comment. Representatives for TWG Global did not respond to a request for comment.

The statement said the department, led by Insurance Commissioner Trinidad Navarro, had previously declined to comment on the matter “due to the ongoing nature of the investigations.”

The Delaware regulator said it needed to issue a statement in response to “the recent drumbeat of inaccuracies being promulgated by individuals with little knowledge of the true facts.” The statement said, “individuals with no knowledge of the complex mechanisms by which these investments were originally misidentified” had wrongfully suggested that Delaware regulator “should have been aware of this deception.”

It is not entirely clear what prompted the insurance department to issue the statement, which was first provided to The Wall Street Journal. But it comes days after The New York Times and Bloomberg News ran articles raising questions about whether insurance regulators in Delaware and other states are keeping pace with the changing dynamics in the insurance industry, which is becoming increasingly influenced by Wall Street.

Insurance analysts and some industry executives have said Delaware regulators should have been more skeptical as to why both Delaware Life and Clear Spring regularly reported a relatively low-level of affiliated investments when many Wall Street-backed competitors were reporting high numbers.

In its statement, the regulator said: “The suggestion that regulators could predict a later scheme hidden from company executives, board members, inside and outside audit firms and rating agencies misses the truth.”

item.title: From Gig Workers to Tycoons, China Is Reaching Into Every Pocket
item.description:
A new joke has been making the rounds on the Chinese internet.

Economists have long said that China’s growth has three engines: investment, consumption and exports. The new engines, the joke goes, are raiding officials’ homes, making the rich pay back taxes and collecting social insurance payments from the poor.

The government needs money to support its rapidly aging population and for costly bets on artificial intelligence. But the economy is in a slump. The result: Chinese people, rich and poor, are feeling the squeeze as Beijing reaches deeper into their pockets to cover its bills.

Hudson Zhou, a 27-year-old freelance illustrator and graphic designer in the southwestern province of Guizhou, saw work dry up as artificial intelligence replaced human-created designs. Zhou, who uses they/them pronouns, had earned only about $4,500 for the year by the end of October — about half as much as in 2025 — but they owe more this year toward the government pension program.

Their pension bill — $1,500 — came out higher than last year because the province raised its minimum contribution for gig workers like Zhou.

China’s economy is in the doldrums, and a property bust has gutted local governments’ revenue from land sales, deepening local government debt.

Workers and employers pay into China’s pension funds, but local governments run them and share some of the cost. Strapped for cash, some have taken money from the funds. In a report released in June 2025, the National Audit Office said 13 provinces had diverted about $6 billion from pension funds to cover government wages and repay debt.

At the same time, the pension system is under strain because of an aging population. Last year only 7.9 million newborns were born in China, roughly half of the average in the 2000s and 2010s.

Beijing also has present-day reasons to encourage people to pay more into the national pension system. If people believe they will have something to rely on in retirement, they might save less and spend their money now, boosting the sluggish economy.

Xu Chenggang, an economist at Stanford, calls the government’s all-out push to collect more social insurance self-defeating. “The economy’s original problem is insufficient domestic demand,” he said. “Now the government squeezes ordinary people to plug its fiscal holes, which makes demand even weaker.”

Last year China’s Supreme People’s Court made it mandatory for employers to pay for employees’ social benefits, which include pensions, health care and unemployment. Businesses have long been required to pay into the system and automatically deduct payments from their employees’ paychecks, just as in the United States, but the law was not always enforced. The court’s decision was met with resistance from small business owners who say they can’t afford the costs and skepticism from workers who fear they will never collect.

This year the Chinese government turned its attention to gig workers, who are estimated by one research center to number some 320 million, or more than 40 percent of the country’s labor force. Only about 70 million of them were enrolled in the basic pension at the end of 2024, according to a government report.

People in the gig economy, which is called flexible employment in China, pay their own social security. The government wants them to pay 20 percent on a base income tied to the provincial average wage. That wage is often far above what gig workers earn, and it rises every year.

To get people to pay, local officials have tried cajoling and coercion. In Yichang, in central Hubei Province, the authorities threw a street festival in October with dancing robots, costumed historical figures and social security planners in matching vests. Elsewhere, the state is steering people toward taking on debt to pay for their retirement. Banks in a few provinces, working with local social security bureaus, offer loans so gig workers can keep paying into the pension fund, with the debt repaid from their future pensions. Some cities also let residents pay with Huabei, a consumer credit platform.

More ominously, the government has also pledged to mine its data to track down people who aren’t contributing. Beijing’s slogan, “leave no one uninsured,” echoes that of the Zero Covid era, “leave no one unquarantined.”

“Where exactly are these people?” Li Zhong, a vice minister of human resources and social security, asked at a news conference last month, referring to people who aren’t contributing. “We have to find them.”

The efforts have drawn widespread criticism on social media. A hashtag on why young people opt out of social insurance drew at least 48 million views on the social media platform Weibo before the topic was blocked in searches.

The Chinese government urgently needs to replenish its pension fund, which experts have said may run out by 2035. It has been raising the retirement age and contribution levels but moving slowly to fix inequalities: Retired government workers receive nearly twice the average pension of private sector retirees and more than 30 times what rural pensioners make.

For Zhou, the visual artist, payments to the pension fund and for medical insurance would amount to $206 a month, or 46 percent of their $450-a-month salary.

Zhou decided to join a growing number of Chinese who have stopped paying into the pension system, which means they won’t get money in retirement.

More concerning for Zhou now is the neighborhood committee that serves as the government’s eyes and ears at the local level.

In 2022 the neighborhood committee tagged Zhou in WeChat groups repeatedly, calling on them and other residents to enroll in medical insurance. Its workers called Zhou’s mother to urge Zhou to enroll. China Mobile, the state-owned wireless carrier, sent automated reminders.

The Chinese government has other ways to compel payment. In some of the biggest cities, residents without local registration can’t buy homes or cars or enroll their children in public schools without contribution records.

Wang, a 24-year-old trainee lawyer in Sichuan Province, has no choice to opt out. (She asked to be identified by only her family name, for fear of government retribution.)

She earns roughly $450 a month and said she had to show proof that her firm pays social insurance for her to obtain a necessary trainee certificate. The social insurance siphons off one-sixth of her pay. She’d rather not pay, she said, partly because it’s too expensive and partly because she questions whether the pension system will still exist by the time she’s old.

Some wealthy Chinese entrepreneurs say they feel like fatty meat the government takes a bite out of when it gets hungry. In recent years, even local police have preyed on businesses, sometimes with trumped-up charges, and extracted payment for debt-plagued local governments.

In July Beijing issued a new rule that demands wealthy Chinese to pay taxes on assets they hold in offshore trusts. Bill, an entrepreneur I’ve known for more than a decade, expects to owe tens of millions of dollars.

Over breakfast overlooking the Imperial Palace in central Tokyo, Bill, who asked to be identified by his English first name because he feared government repercussions, described his confusion and resignation.

He has lived in Hong Kong for more than a decade, holds a Hong Kong passport and says he has paid taxes there for years. Under the new rule, he said, none of that may matter.

He fears making the payment would amount to accepting Chinese tax residency, leaving his income and investments outside China open to taxation later.

“Being born in China has become original sin,” he said.

item.title: China’s A.I. Ambitions Are Running Into a Money Problem
item.description:
As the United States and China vie for artificial intelligence supremacy, Chinese tech companies are facing a mounting challenge: finding the money to keep up.

Like their American rivals, China’s A.I. start-ups face soaring costs to train increasingly powerful models. But while Anthropic raised more than $80 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering this week, its Chinese competitors face a far more unforgiving financial landscape.

Venture capital investment in China lags far behind that of the United States. Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent, three tech giants backing some of China’s leading A.I. companies, are grappling with negative cash flows. And investor enthusiasm for A.I. has soured. Since the end of July, China’s STAR 50 index, its version of the Nasdaq, has plunged 43 percent in a deeper sell-off than the recent downturn in American tech stocks.

China’s biggest tech companies are expected to double capital spending this year to $139 billion, even though the revenue from their A.I. labs covers less than 8 percent of that amount, according to Rhodium Group, a research firm. It forecasts that spending could top $193 billion in 2027.

“When you look at their numbers, it looks like they’re running on a treadmill that’s speeding up and getting harder to run,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, who specializes in China’s technology and industrial policies.

Much of the debate over China’s ability to compete in A.I. has focused on American export controls to restrict Chinese access to advanced semiconductors. Chinese A.I. labs have found costly workarounds, including renting data centers in Southeast Asia equipped with Nvidia chips. The Trump administration said this week it was moving forward with new rules to close that loophole.

But money might prove an equally formidable obstacle. Even if Chinese companies can find the chips they need, they must raise enough capital to buy them and finance the rising cost of developing frontier models.

Logan Wright, a partner at Rhodium Group who co-wrote a report on China’s A.I. financing, said those financial constraints “will be probably more decisive” than the chip shortage in the long term.

“The big problem is that the revenue mismatch with the Chinese models relative to capex is arguably more extreme than the U.S. case,” Mr. Wright said.

American A.I. companies spend roughly five to six times what their Chinese counterparts do, but bring in substantially more money. China’s six leading A.I. firms collectively generate about one-tenth the combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization.

China’s embrace of open-source A.I. has made that imbalance even harder to overcome.

By allowing developers to use and modify their models freely, Chinese companies have accelerated the global spread of their technology. But that strategy has also undermined their ability to profit from it. Companies can charge for access, only to see rivals offer the same technology at lower prices. Fierce price wars have squeezed profits further.

Z.ai, a Chinese A.I. start-up, learned that lesson in August when it released its latest open-source model, GLM-5.3 Flash. The company halved prices for two weeks to entice users to run the model on Z.ai’s servers rather than their own. But competitors quickly moved in.

By November, roughly 20 rival providers were charging less than Z.ai for access to its own technology, according to Open Router, a platform connecting users with A.I. models.

“Your own pricing power is lost during this process,” said Cheryl Wu, a researcher at GovAI, a think tank.

“No one has figured out how to make money off consumers,” said Rui Ma, a technology investor, referring to Chinese A.I. start-ups.

Another obstacle worsens China’s financing problems: access to advanced Nvidia chips, the gold standard for training the most powerful A.I. models.

From 2022 to June 2026, American companies possessed computing capacity equivalent to about 20 million Nvidia H100 chips, compared with roughly 2.6 million in China, some of it acquired through smuggling, according to EpochAI.

On Goofish, a Chinese secondhand online marketplace, sellers have advertised Nvidia’s DGX B300, an A.I. supercomputing server, for nearly $3 million — about eight times the U.S. price. Asking prices have reportedly quintupled since the start of the year, underscoring the premium Chinese companies must pay for advanced computing power.

The squeeze could worsen. Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief last week amid an investigation into a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman, was a powerful advocate of doing business with China. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China, a deal that President Trump had previously permitted at Mr. Huang’s urging. The company also said it had established an export control oversight committee.

To reduce their dependence on American technology, Chinese developers are adapting their systems to run on chips made by Huawei, the Chinese telecommunications and electronics company leading the country’s chip charge.

Liang Wenfeng, chief executive of DeepSeek, the Chinese start-up that stunned Silicon Valley by developing a powerful A.I. model at a fraction of the expected cost, said Huawei’s technology is only about two years behind Nvidia’s.

But the gap remains consequential. DeepSeek would need four times as many Huawei 950 chips to match the performance of a single advanced Nvidia GB300 chip, Mr. Liang said, according to a leaked transcript of his call with investors, excerpts from which Chinese media outlets published. Huawei also lacks sufficient production capacity, he added.

“We simply can’t afford to train the largest models available right now,” he said. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.

Yet China’s A.I. industry has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to do more with less. Chinese researchers have pioneered techniques to train and run powerful models more efficiently. Silicon Valley has accused Chinese firms of copying leading American technologies through a process called distillation, reducing the time needed to build foundational models with expensive computing infrastructure.

For China’s A.I. companies, finding investors willing to bankroll the competition is increasingly difficult.

DeepSeek, which has raised more than $20 billion, is preparing for an initial public offering in Shanghai early next year, according to Chinese media reports. Its investors include Tencent, the battery maker CATL and state-backed investment funds.

Few competitors have access to such deep pockets.

China’s venture capital industry has been shrinking since 2021 and though it has recovered slightly in the third quarter, it is still a fraction of its American counterpart. Banks are lending to China’s tech giants, but they are more cautious with smaller A.I. labs. Credit growth has fallen to historic lows, and the central bank governor has called for slower, “higher-quality” lending.

Foreign investment has also dried up. U.S. dollar-denominated investment funds in China have plunged partly because Washington has barred American venture capital from certain advanced Chinese technologies.

In 2025, private A.I. investment in China totaled $12.4 billion, compared with $280 billion in the United States, according to the Stanford A.I. Index.

Han Lin, the China country director for the Asia Group, an advisory firm, said China had exceptional engineering talent and a government capable of mobilizing enormous resources for strategic industries.

But he added, “What frontier technology also needs is harder to mobilize — risk capital that can absorb failure.”

Even the public markets, a lifeline for cash-hungry start-ups, are becoming less welcoming. Amid the sell-off, the Chinese authorities have instructed some companies to delay or suspend planned public listings, according to Cailian Press, a Chinese business publication, suggesting Beijing is concerned about an A.I. investment bubble.

China has announced investment funds to support A.I., but much of the money has gone toward semiconductors rather than companies developing large language models.

Government investors face many of the same constraints as private ones. Wang Renxuan, an assistant finance professor at the China Europe International Business School in Shanghai, said government funds also need a credible path to returns.

Erik Walenza, a Shanghai-based managing partner at Asia Growth Partners, a consultancy advising on A.I., said it was difficult to see how Chinese A.I. companies could make their finances work “without a lot of sustained government financing.”

The challenge, he added, is not only whether Chinese engineers can build models to rival America’s but also how much of the financial burden the government is prepared to shoulder.

“It becomes more of a political will question, of how much sacrifice are we willing to make to compete in this area,” Mr. Walenza said.

item.title: Is an ‘A.I. Agent’ Coming for Our Sourdough Starter?
item.description:
Before opening his eight Upside Pizza slice shops in New York City, Noam Grossman studied with the sourdough master Anthony Falco, and has faithfully kept his original starter alive and bubbling. Naturally leavened dough, he believes, holds the secret to Upside’s signature crisp-chewy crust.

But last week, in a basement near the Port Authority Bus Terminal, Mr. Grossman grew increasingly agitated as he realized the stuff he was about to pour into a Hobart mixer could upend all that.

Leaven, a laboratory-grown product, is a shelf-stable powder that eliminates the need for the live sourdough starter that has long been the pride and preoccupation of craft bakers.

“Now that I know what it does, it feels weird to hold in my hand,” Mr. Grossman said. “This is like an A.I. agent. It feels like an existential threat to thousands of years of tradition.”

Invented by two Colorado microbiologists who are also home bakers, Leaven arrived in stores in June. But it has been quietly adopted by some of the nation’s top bakers and pizza makers over the past two years.

When added to flour and water, the microbes in Leaven begin the work of fermentation, and can carry it out it more reliably than notoriously temperamental sourdough starters. It does not shorten or replace the fermentation process — the dough still has to rise and proof as usual — but it does jump-start it.

Still, many bakers I spoke to are leery of Leaven. In professional baking, prestige is often attached to the most time-consuming, challenging and traditional methods. The mystique of live sourdough starter is the basis of the craft baking movement that took hold in the United States in the 1970s and built national brands like Panera, La Brea and Izzio.

“The emotional connection is real,” said Chad Robertson, a pioneer of the movement who founded the Tartine bakeries and just opened Altbau in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. Serious bread bakers sometimes travel with their starter, exposing it to local strains of the wild yeasts that give sourdough breads their complex flavors. After nurturing his starter in Los Angeles for a decade, he took it to Australia, Germany, Mexico and Spain, while studying and teaching. “And then to Costa Rica for a month to surf,” he said.

Although doubtful about Leaven’s ability to replicate the effect of live starter, he was curious. “If it works,” he said. “It would be the holy grail.”

Only a few Leaven users agreed to speak about the product. Others declined, including some large companies that are testing it for use in fast-food sandwiches and supermarket breads. (Some industrial bakers around the world are already using similar products.)

Scarr Pimentel, the founder of Scarr’s, the high-profile Manhattan pizzeria that first became famous for using house-milled flour and natural leavening, confirmed that he uses Leaven in all his crusts, both on the Lower East Side and in Las Vegas, with no noticeable difference.

“It’s the ultimate hack,” said Christiano Wennmann, Scarr’s head baker, who said he had kept quiet for fear that every pizza maker would start using it. “I’ve been gatekeeping it, to be honest.”

Mr. Wennmann said Leaven’s consistent results make it irresistible for a business with multiple locations and employees. “It removes a variable from a very complicated process,” he said.

Leaven is the first consumer product to encapsulate not only strains of wild yeast, but also the beneficial bacteria that live in an active starter. It’s also gluten-free, unlike a flour-based starter.

Marc Magliozzi has been fixated on improving his pizza for the 16 years Dozzino in Hoboken, N.J., has been open. He started with commercial yeast, moved to a biga (an Italian sourdough method) and then to Leaven. He said it produces a less sour flavor than live starter, but preserves the chew and umami of long-fermented dough.

“I never really wanted pizza crust to be sour,” he said, citing the tang of the tomato sauce on top. “In 10 years I think the whole sourdough pizza thing will be over.”

Still the popularity of sourdough — which generally makes tastier, more substantial and more digestible breads — marches on. Three of Time magazine’s Best New Inventions of 2026 are sourdough-related: the Sourdough Sidekick, a countertop appliance from King Arthur Flour that automatically builds a starter; Dough Dissolve, an enzyme-based cleaning product; and Leaven. It is moving into sweet baking: Sweetgreen has just released a sourdough chocolate-chip cookie nationwide.

But the term “sourdough,” like “slow-fermented” and “naturally leavened,” isn’t regulated in any way. Anything can wear the label, from supermarket white bread with a dash of commercial sour flavoring to the $60 organic rye loaf from an Austrian baker that recently made a splashy debut in New York.

During the pandemic, many home cooks fell for the siren song of sourdough. But given the work of feeding, airing and measuring a starter — not to mention the constant pressure to use it up — many (including me) found that a starter can feel like yet another domestic burden.

Just like the packets of dry yeast that most home bakers use, Leaven can be kept in the pantry and used anytime. It still took me 14 hours of proofing, stretching and folding, but the focaccia I made with it tasted better — sweeter and wheatier — than the yeast-risen version I usually bake.

Leaven’s founders, the microbiologists Cameron Martino and James Gaffney, are also avid home brewers. In an interview, Mr. Martino said that dozens of brewer’s yeasts are available, each producing a distinct style, like ales, lagers and lambics. So, they wondered, why there was only one kind of baker’s yeast on the market?

Virtually all commercial dough in the United States is made with active dry yeast, the dehydrated, domesticated version of a single yeast strain that was isolated by the Fleischmann’s company in the 1930s. That strain was selected for its quick-rising qualities: It generates the most carbon dioxide in the least time, producing a puffy loaf with a soft crumb.

But, Mr. Martino said, “you lose flavors, textures and other alternatives when you push everything into gas.”

Long fermentation with certain microbes gives sourdoughs their characteristic taste and texture. When flour and water are exposed to air and mixed with water, the bacteria and yeasts in a starter (or in a pouch of Leaven) get to work, breaking down the flour’s carbohydrates into sugars that they can eat. The bacteria are beneficial lactobacilli, the same microbes that give dry-cured meats, aged cheeses and long-fermented kimchi their umami-rich flavor.

I found it difficult to wrap my mind around how wild yeasts and living bacteria can exist in a shelf-stable product. I put this question to Scott Wiener, a New York pizza expert who teaches classes and leads tours. “If you put a rhinoceros in a zoo, it’s still a rhinoceros, right?” he said.

I pushed back, pointing out that a rhinoceros in a zoo is still noticeably alive. Is this rhinoceros, perhaps, in an artificially induced coma? “Exactly,” he said.

Back in the basement at Upside Pizza, two days after Mr. Grossman mixed the dough, it was time to bake two identical pies: one with his starter and one with Leaven.

For a first outing, the Leaven crust came out quite well — soft and stretchy, charred well on the bottom and able to hold a New York fold. Asked if he thought he could create a perfect replica of his crust with Leaven, Mr. Grossman said yes.

And if he could, would he?

“Absolutely not,” he said. The starter he uses is more than 10 years old, and has been handed off from one pizzaiolo to another, all of them successful.

“It’s not going anywhere,” he said.

item.title: Stocks Often Prosper After an Abrupt C.E.O. Exit. Is Nvidia Different?
item.description:
Nvidia shareholders have lost so much money that the sum is practically unfathomable: around $2 trillion from late October through Thursday. Only Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon — and, for a brief time on Thursday, Anthropic — are even worth that much.

Nvidia’s vanished stock market value was roughly equivalent, in dollar terms, to simultaneously wiping three corporate giants, like JPMorgan, Exxon Mobil and United Health Care, off the face of the earth.

Not all of this colossal loss of wealth can be attributed to the forced departure of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder. But, undoubtedly, a great deal of Nvidia’s stock market plight stems from his unceremonious exit.

No wonder a swelling group of Nvidia loyalists is agitating for his return to the company. Mr. Huang said on Tuesday that he would be “honored to answer these calls and return as C.E.O.,” but the company’s board quickly made it clear that it would not welcome him back. So I wouldn’t count on Mr. Huang’s imminent return.

Yet this needn’t be a continuing calamity for Nvidia’s stock. History suggests that no executive at a mature company is irreplaceable, even if he is a global celebrity and a firm founder. After the initial shock and once a permanent replacement is in place, many companies recover in the stock market, several studies show.

Every company is different, however. The role of Mr. Huang at Nvidia poses special problems in assessing the company’s chances of prospering without him.

It’s not merely that he occupied a central position in what has arguably been the most important company in the most important industry in the world economy. Mr. Huang was also a pivotal player in U.S.-Chinese corporate relations, and the extent of his involvement in the supply of Nvidia chips and computing power to companies based in China isn’t yet known.

“Nvidia’s sales to China could be worth 20 percent or 30 percent” of the company’s peak stock market value, Aswath Damodaran, a New York University finance professor, said in an interview. That’s a big caveat, he said. It could be an exception to the rule that a stock like Nvidia ought to be solid enough to recover fully after a change in leadership.

Without Mr. Huang’s China connections, and amid national security concerns, investigations, congressional hearings and a harsher regulatory climate, “it may already be too late to restore all the lost value” coming from Nvidia’s sales, direct and indirect, to China, he said.

While much remains to be discovered, the basics of the Nvidia story are widely known. It designs advanced chips that power artificial intelligence, which made it an earnings machine, producing astonishing profits that, until its recent debacle, buoyed the entire stock market.

The company also served as a kind of central bank for the A.I. industry, pumping hundreds of billions of dollars into aspiring competitors, suppliers and customers, as my colleagues, Maureen Farrell and Rob Copeland, have written. For example, it committed to invest $10 billion in Anthropic before that A.I. giant’s initial public offering this week.

Nvidia remains a financial powerhouse — with revenue of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion in the three months through October, according to its latest disclosures on Tuesday. Both figures exceeded Wall Street’s expectations, and Nvidia projected revenue in the current quarter to be even larger, about $130 billion. Its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has been running the company on an interim basis since Nov. 12. That’s when Mr. Huang resigned.

He stepped down in the wake of a New York Times report that he had an affair with an employee at Nvidia, as well as with Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence has determined is an asset for Chinese intelligence. On Monday, the Trump administration moved to block the sale of advanced chips to data centers of the type run by Ms. Huang. She started a Singapore company called Megaspeed that is under investigation over allegations of smuggling chips to China. Chinese officials have denied that Ms. Huang is a spy for China. In his public comments in China, President Trump played down the episode.

The vast literature on the stock market effects of abrupt C.E.O. departures fails to offer many definitive lessons.

One thing that is clear, however, is that hasty executive exits tend to upset the stock market over short periods. One study of 30 such cases by BCA Research, an independent financial research firm, found that over the last three decades, 70 percent of the companies underperformed their benchmark significantlyover the following month.

In a separate study, Bespoke Investment Group, another independent research firm, examined how stocks performed one year after the chief executives were pushed out by their boards. It examined 30 cases that occurred within the last 10 years and found that, on average, the companies’ shares were down 12 percent one year later.

There was a silver lining in the Bespoke study. Of the six companies in the group in which the chief executives had to leave for what Bespoke called “bad behavior” involving “an inappropriate personal relationship,” their average stock was up 12 percent.

In an interview, Paul Hickey, a co-founder of Bespoke, called those returns “somewhat positive but not dramatic, because the market in that period was positive.” In fact, the S&P 500 over the last 10 years gained an annualized 13 percent, according to FactSet.

Yet another study, by Commons Capital, a wealth management firm, focused on 15 corporate founders who left their companies for a variety of reasons since 1985. It found that although the stock shares of most companies declined in the 12 months after a C.E.O. departure, a few well-known companies prospered.

Perhaps the most prominent was Apple, whose top executive, Steve Jobs, departed twice: in 1985, when he was pushed out by the Apple board; and in 2011, when he resigned because of the pancreatic cancer that led to his death. Both times, Apple stock soared over the following 12 months. But Mr. Jobs’s first successor, John Sculley, was himself forced out in 1993 when the company’s fortunes were ebbing. The second coming of Mr. Jobs culminated in the creation of the iPhone, the sleek gadget that transformed the world and turned around Apple’s fortunes. Mr. Jobs’s second successor, Tim Cook, never pretended to be the creative maestro that Mr. Jobs was, but Mr. Cook led Apple to tremendous gains, as an efficient and mature company, until resigning as chief executive and becoming chairman this year.

I ran the numbers on FactSet: From Aug. 24, 2011, when Mr. Cook became chief executive, until April 20, 2026, when he announced his resignation, Apple shares returned 24.3 percent, annualized, including dividends, compared with 15.2 percent for the S&P 500.

Nvidia, at this stage, seems to be “a fairly mature company with a good pipeline of products and a deep bench,” Mr. Damodaran said. “It could well resemble Apple under Tim Cook,” if not for the issues with China and the turbulence of the A.I. industry itself.

So what should one conclude from all this? Predicting how Nvidia will fare is a hazardous task. Whether Nvidia shares soar once again will depend on very specific issues that I won’t even try to assess in advance.

As an investor, I don’t even attempt to judge individual securities. Instead, I hold a part of the entire stock and bond markets through low-cost index funds and try to prosper over long periods when the economy does. What’s happened to Nvidia shares over the last month only reinforces the case.

Nvidia was the biggest company in the stock market until recently, and its decline is dragging down broad index returns. But at least these losses are being buffered by other stocks and bonds.

The future of A.I. and of the stock market won’t depend on just one company — not on Nvidia and probably not on Anthropic, which began trading shares to the public on Thursday. But Anthropic warned in its prospectus that its A.I. has the potential to destroy humanity.

Even well-diversified investors have plenty to worry about.

item.title: Anthropic’s Banner Debut Not Enough to Stop Slide in Stock Market
item.description:
The blockbuster market debut for Anthropic, one of the biggest players in artificial intelligence, was not enough to turn the broader tide for stocks, with major indexes slumping at the end of another tumultuous week for investors.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq benchmarks were on course for their worst weeks in well over a year, dragged down by technology stocks as traders question the durability of the A.I. boom.

The S&P 500 has fallen over 5 percent through Thursday, the worst week for the index since April 2025, when the market convulsed in response to the announcement of President Trump’s sweeping global tariffs. Futures markets suggested that stocks would continue to slide when U.S. trading opens on Friday.

Anthropic’s stock, after surging by double-digit percentages in its trading debut on Thursday, itself slipped 8 percent premarket.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The declines have persisted despite generally favorable reactions from analysts and investors to the week’s major events, billed ahead of time as pivotal to the A.I. trade that has powered the market for months but has faltered more recently.

Nvidia’s earnings report on Tuesday helped to calm fears of a slowdown in growth of the A.I. build-out, with the giant chip maker raising its profit forecast. It was a brief respite for the company, which is reeling after the resignation of its larger-than-life chief executive, Jensen Huang, following revelations that he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials determined was feeding information to Beijing.

Then on Thursday, Anthropic jumped more than 17 percent in its first day of trading, achieving a trillion-dollar valuation after setting a record for the largest public offering in history. Robust demand for the shares of the maker of the Claude chatbot suggested that investors were still optimistic about aspects of the A.I. industry.

But the rest of the market has continued to slide. The S&P 500 has fallen for six straight trading days, its longest losing streak since April 2024. Every sector of the index is lower for the week, led by tech shares. The Nasdaq Composite is on course for a loss of 5 percent this week.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

“Unfortunately, there isn’t an obvious catalyst or event to improve sentiment as we head into year-end,” said Stuart Kaiser, an analyst at Citi, adding that “there are no clear signposts to swing the pendulum.”

Traders tend to book profits in the run-up to Thanksgiving, mindful that markets slow into the end of the year, which can make it harder to move in and out of positions. There is also typically trepidation around this time about holding large positions through year’s end.

Nvidia has fallen nearly 40 percent since the S&P 500 peaked in early October, accounting for roughly half of the 8 percent drop in the index over that period, according to Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist for LPL Financial. Nvidia has been “the big factor” weighing on the market, he said, emblematic of “the broader fear over an A.I. slowdown.” The chip maker’s stock was down, again, in premarket trading on Friday.

Chip makers and related stocks were also weighed down by a report released on Thursday by Hunterbrook, a short-selling firm that profits from bets against companies, that claimed Advanced Micro Devices had supplied U.S.-blacklisted Chinese companies with updates to keep its chips running. (AMD said that the claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships.”)

Anthropic’s newly listed stock soared as much as 38 percent in early trading on Thursday, but as the day progressed, the air came out of the company’s ballooning price. Its shares ended the day up 17 percent, at $97 a share.

That’s still a healthy rise from its I.P.O. price of $83 per share, but suggested a more restrained optimism for the company’s prospects than the initial flurry of trades.

Still, analyst recommendations for the Anthropic, collated by the market data firm FactSet, show bullish expectations for the future. Ben Reitzes at Melius Research represents the high-water mark, with an initial price target of $155 per share. At the other end of the spectrum is Patrick Walravens at Citizens, with a target of $125.

But the CBOE Vix Volatility index, a measure known as the market’s “fear gauge,” which measure investors’ expectations of volatility over the next 30 days, recently rose just above its peak in the whipsaw aftermath of the midterm elections, a sign of market jitters.

“There’s been a lot of talk about whether the A.I. trade had gotten ahead of itself,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, who pointed to Nvidia’s strong earnings and the initial rise in Anthropic’s shares as “notable” signs for investors. “That doesn’t settle every valuation debate,” he added, “but it’s pretty strong affirmation that the market is not ready to walk away from the trade just yet.”

item.title: Can Anthropic Revive the A.I. Trade?
item.description:
Andrew here. At the DealBook Summit this week, my colleagues Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan led a remarkable panel on the midterms and what they mean for 2028.

The panelists included Stacey Abrams, David Axelrod, Alyssa Farah Griffin, Morris Katz, Dan Senor and David Urban — three Democrats and three Republicans, at least two of whom have worked for President Trump. What made it fascinating was how little anyone held back. It was an unfiltered look at how campaigns are quietly strategizing for the next cycle — and yes, at times it got heated. You can watch it here.

Anthropic just pulled off the biggest I.P.O. ever and minted billions in paper profits for its founders, employees and pre-offering backers. Yet investors seem to want more.

Shares in the artificial intelligence giant are down about 9 percent in premarket trading, and S&P 500 futures are in the red. It’s a sign that there are still significant hurdles for Anthropic and for the broader A.I. industry.

By the numbers:

Anthropic now has a market value of about $1.27 trillion — or, on a fully diluted stock basis, nearly $1.8 trillion.

The company raised about $120 billion from the I.P.O.

Anthropic’s offering minted huge winners, beyond its seven founders:

Even recently hired employees enjoyed windfalls: A staff member awarded options on $1 million of stock in 2024 would now, on average, be sitting on about $66 million of stock when it vests, The Times calculates. (Unlike most I.P.O.s, employees were able to start selling their holdings right away.)

The lead underwriters, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, are set to collect about $113 million each from the offering.

Anthropic’s venture capital backers are set to receive generational returns: Spark Capital, the only investment firm with a seat on the company’s board, invested $75 million in the company in 2023 — and now sits on a stake valued at $17.1 billion.

Others sitting on windfalls include the hedge fund billionaire Gregory Jensen and the tech mogul Dustin Moskovitz (who told The Times that he’s worried about A.I. safety and won’t personally profit from selling Anthropic shares in the open market.)

Ravi Mhatre, a founder of Lightspeed Venture Partners and a major investor in the company, told DealBook’s Michael de la Merced, “Anthropic as a public company creates more of an understanding with the public markets that there is a viable business model.”

Yet Anthropic’s I.P.O. hasn’t totally allayed investor fears about the A.I. boom. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.2 percent yesterday, as the offering failed to reignite confidence in A.I. stocks, which have slumped amid concerns about valuations, spending and the turmoil at Nvidia.

(It didn’t help that shares in the chip maker AMD tanked yesterday after the short seller Hunterbrook accused the company of supplying U.S.-blacklisted Chinese companies with processors. AMD has disputed the report.)

Anthropic still faces headwinds, including the $900 billion it’s projected to spend on data centers and computing power in the next several years. And while its A.I. models are considered among the most advanced, it faces competition from almost-as-capable open-weight models that cost far less to use.

That raises questions about what lies ahead for OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, which is set to go public next year.

Chipmakers face scrutiny over their China links. California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, has opened an investigation into whether Nvidia’s advanced chips or their trade secrets have been transferred to China. But in a sign of how complicated it might be to police the sector, lawmakers in Washington disclosed that the Commerce Department had approved sales of more than 800,000 artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies, some with military ties.

The White House replaces its top cybersecurity official. The official, Sean Cairncross, left his position as national cyber director days after a series of technological outages grounded commercial air traffic in the U.S., and disrupted banking and email services. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, will replace him.

A regulator rebukes companies tied to Mark Walter. The Delaware Department of Insurance said that two insurance firms controlled by Walter, the billionaire owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, had misled it and other regulators about billions of dollars in assets they held that were investments in other businesses tied to him. Separately, Walter is nearing a deal to sell the Los Angeles Sparks of the WNBA for $750 million, Sportico reports, citing unnamed sources.

Grand Theft Auto VI pops off. Take-Two Interactive’s update to the action-adventure video game franchise has posted Hollywood blockbuster-like numbers, selling a reported 24.6 million copies for over $2.3 billion in its first two days. Consider: It takes up to an estimated 100 hours to complete G.T.A. VI, the “Super Bowl of video games,” which is a sort of crime simulator and cartoonish sendup of American life set in a sexy, neon stand-in for Miami. That has left schools and businesses bracing for absences with so-called G.T.A. flu.

Anthropic was seemingly everywhere in midtown Manhattan yesterday. The company’s black-and-white logo and its advertising tagline — “What we make of this moment, will make this moment” — blanketed billboard after eye-popping billboard in Times Square.

A few blocks up, Morgan Stanley and Barclays, two banks that helped Anthropic go public, wrapped their buildings in giant scrolling text, celebrating the record-breaking I.P.O.

The splashy party drew throngs of TV crews, some A.I. protesters and plenty of gawkers. On the corner of Broadway and 46th Street, one confused man asked DealBook’s Bernhard Warner, “What are they selling, anyhow?”

At Broadway and 43rd Street, the message became clearer: Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s C.E.O., appeared on a screen several stories high outside the Nasdaq MarketSite headquarters, talking up the potential of Claude, Anthropic’s chatbot, and warning of A.I.’s wider risks.

The charitable foundation run jointly by the embattled former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, is a potentially significant asset if their marriage goes sideways.

Already one of the country’s largest private charities, it has grown much bigger recently, Theodore Schleifer reports for DealBook.

The foundation has nearly $13 billion in assets, according to a tax return from 2025 obtained by The New York Times. Its assets surged by about 40 percent that year.

The Huangs are co-presidents of the entity, called the Jen-hsun & Lori Huang Foundation.

It’s not known if the couple plans to divorce. But the state of their 41-year marriage has been the subject of speculation ever since Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful.

Huang resigned as C.E.O. of Nvidia last week after reports of his affairs with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese asset, as well as an executive at his company. At the DealBook Summit on Wednesday, tech leaders expressed empathy for Huang.

A split would be costly for Huang. His net worth currently stands at $122 billion, according to Bloomberg. High-profile divorces of several tech founders have created a class of female billionaire philanthropists, including MacKenzie Scott and Melinda French Gates.

Most of the Huang Foundation’s spending in 2025 went to an Nvidia partner. The foundation disclosed in its tax filing that it prepaid for $350 million in computing power that it is in the process of awarding to nonprofits.

That compute was purchased from CoreWeave, which Nvidia previously disclosed had sold $108.3 million of computing capacity to the Huang’s foundation.

In the A.I. race between the U.S. and China, much of the focus has been on access to advanced computer chips. For example, the Trump administration said on Monday it would close a loophole that allowed workarounds for Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s semiconductors.

But increasingly, there’s another factor that threatens to throttle the growth of Chinese tech companies: Money.

China can’t keep pace with U.S. capital markets, Sui-Lee Wee and Li You report for The Times:

Venture capital investment in China lags far behind that of the United States. Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent, three tech giants backing some of China’s leading A.I. companies, are grappling with negative cash flows. And investor enthusiasm for A.I. has soured. Since the end of July, China’s STAR 50 index, its version of the Nasdaq, has plunged 43 percent in a deeper sell-off than the recent downturn in American tech stocks.

China’s biggest tech companies are expected to double capital spending this year to $139 billion, even though the revenue from their A.I. labs covers less than 8 percent of that amount, according to Rhodium Group, a research firm. It forecasts that spending could top $193 billion in 2027.

Part of the challenge is the business model. Many Chinese companies have embraced open source A.I., which means that when they charge for access, they may soon see competitors offer the same model at a lower price.

China’s six leading A.I. firms together generate about one-tenth the combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization.

The cost of compute is rising with U.S. chip restrictions. “We simply can’t afford to train the largest models available right now,” Liang Wenfeng, C.E.O. of DeepSeek, recently told investors, according to a leaked transcript of the call.

Deals

Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing company it bought in 2021 for $12 billion, to Bending Spoons, an Italian acquirer of older tech businesses, for about $3.7 billion. (CNBC)

Sanofi is reportedly weighing a takeover bid for Insmed, a U.S. maker of treatments for respiratory diseases, with a market value of $31.6 billion. (Bloomberg)

“Lenders Aim to Bar SpaceX from Launching $40bn of Chips Into Orbit” (FT)

Politics, policy and regulation

The Senate passed a bill to speed up the federal permitting process for energy projects and to require data centers to pay for the energy they use, which could double by 2030. (NYT, CNBC)

Investment accounts tied to President Trump bought shares in companies that recently scored federal contracts or that grew closer to the White House. (CNBC)

Law firms that gave the White House free legal work are preparing for inquiries by congressional Democrats. (FT)

Best of the rest

Americans have access to ever more powerful technology, but many are feeling increasingly powerless. (NYT)

The two chairmen of the white-shoe law firm Sullivan & Cromwell, including Robert Giuffra, one of Trump’s personal lawyers, plan to step down in 2028. (WSJ)

“That ‘SNL’ Sister Sketch: It’s More Like Nonfiction” (NYT)

item.title: Savings Bonds Offer Enticing Rates. You Need to Prove Your Identity First.
item.description:
Newly issued government savings bonds that guard against inflation are currently paying 5.51 percent interest rates, far better than the highest rate available on federally insured savings accounts.

But since Oct. 28, the Treasury Department has required that customers use a private service, ID.me, to verify their identities. Until they do so, customers can’t get access to the federal TreasuryDirect website to buy bonds or see their holdings online.

Not everyone is thrilled about the new procedure.

John Ferreira, a retiree and Treasury Direct user in Kensington, Calif., said he received an email from the site in late October, telling him to create an account within a week with ID.me to access his holdings, including I bonds and a two-year Treasury note. He had been logging on infrequently, he said, with a username, password and an account number. Sometimes, he was asked to answer a few security questions.

Mr. Ferreira, 81, said he found the email suspicious, because warnings to take swift action on money matters are considered “a tell-tale sign” of financial fraud. He said he wondered: “Is it a scam?” Although the email proved legitimate, Mr. Ferreira said he still objected to having TreasuryDirect “hold my bonds hostage unless I used a third-party app.”

In a statement, Wes Turbeville, a company senior vice president, said: “We want every ID.me authentication to go smoothly and recognize that anything less can be frustrating, especially if the user is unfamiliar with online identity proofing processes.” He added that users also have the option to prove their identities using a “live, secure” video call on a computer and can reach support at help.id.me.

Here’s what to know if you are a TreasuryDirect customer or want to become one.

The TreasuryDirect website says ID.me offers a “faster, more secure experience” than its traditional, in-house log on system. Most users can verify their identities in under 10 minutes, TreasuryDirect says. Once they do so, logging on takes just seconds for subsequent visits.

A Treasury spokeswoman, Athina Lawson, said in an email that ID.me is a federally certified identity verification provider and that the change “provides additional safeguards to protect customers’ personal and financial information and reduce the risk of unauthorized account access.”

ID.me was founded in 2010 by an Army veteran, Blake Hall, who saw another veteran hand over his discharge paperwork to a store employee to claim a military discount, according to its website. Mr. Hall thought there should be a better way for people to prove their identities without disclosing personal information, according to its website. The company now offers identity verification services for about two dozen federal websites as well as to many state government agencies and private businesses to confirm that online users are who they say they are and prevent fraud.

For many federal websites, including Social Security, Medicare and Veterans Affairs, ID.me is often offered as an option alongside Login.gov, a government-administered online identity verification service.

In the case of TreasuryDirect, however, ID.me is the sole option available. Ms. Lawson, the Treasury Department spokeswoman, said the department was also evaluating using Login.gov.

The Internal Revenue Service, which is part of Treasury, added Login.gov as an option in addition to ID.me for its websites a few weeks ago, an I.R.S. spokesman said.

To use ID.me, users need government identification like a driver’s license or passport, their Social Security number and, typically, a smartphone with a camera. You may be asked for photo verification using your cellphone, the Treasury Direct website says, so the service can confirm the user is the same person shown on the ID.

Users who don’t have smartphones may need extra time to complete verification. Jonathan Kahn, 70, of New York City, said he uses a so-called VoIP line, which connects voice calls over the internet, but which turned out to be incompatible with ID.me. It took several hours, including time waiting for two online help sessions, before the issue was identified, he said; eventually, he was authorized using an alternative method.

Users can contact ID.me for online help if they have trouble.

Some privacy groups have raised concerns about the service’s data retention policies. ID.me’s website said it may retain biometric data, such as “facial geometry recognition,” for as little as 24 hours or as long as three years, depending on the department using the service. The timing can also vary depending on the requirements of the first agency a customer uses to verify their identity with the service.

According to TreasuryDirect’s website, ID.me acts “solely as an identity provider,” and neither TreasuryDirect nor ID.me “sells, rents, or shares your personal information” for marketing or advertising purposes.

Two senators, Ron Wyden of Oregon and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, both Democrats, raised concerns about the move to ID.me in a letter on Oct. 27 to top Treasury and I.R.S. officials. They said that the transition was “needlessly rushed” and that savings bonds are primarily held by older Americans, “who may lack the digital proficiency to quickly transition between complicated online systems.” They also said the rationale for expanded use of ID.me was “unclear,” asserting that Login.gov meets necessary security standards.

Ms. Lawson said TreasuryDirect began notifying customers of the change on Aug. 3, using email, the TreasuryDirect website, and messages displayed when users logged on, before beginning the transition to ID.me on Sept. 13. The site also published answers to frequently asked questions on its website.

The senators had asked that the switch be delayed until after the 2027 tax filing season so that users could continue to use their old log on to obtain tax documents, such as interest statements for bonds redeemed this year.

TreasuryDirect says ID.me offers the “simplest” way to get tax documents like 1099-INT forms showing interest paid, but users can also ask to have the forms mailed by calling TreasuryDirect’s customer support at 844-284-2676.

Rates on series I savings bonds, known as I bonds, can change every six months based on inflation. New I bonds are paying 5.51 percent through April 30, 2027.

In comparison, the highest rate available on high-yield, federally insured savings accounts is just over 4 percent, according to Bankrate.

The rate on I bonds is a combination of a fixed rate, set when the bond is issued and lasting for the bond’s 30-year life, and a variable rate that changes every six months — on May 1 and Nov. 1 — based on the Consumer Price Index. The variable rate applies to new bonds as well as to older bonds that are still earning interest.

Individuals can buy $10,000 in I bonds per year. (The option to buy an extra $5,000 in bonds with your tax refund was eliminated last year).

You can’t redeem the bonds for at least one year. And if you cash them in before five years, there’s a penalty — you’ll forfeit the last three months’ worth of interest.

Interest earned on I bonds is exempt from state and local income taxes but is subject to federal tax, although you can wait to pay until you cash in the bonds.

You don’t have to use the TreasuryDirect website to manage paper bonds. You can ask your bank if it will cash them, or you can fill out a form and mail them to the Treasury Department.
